analysis.one_liner: Creates federal loan guarantees, direct loans, and military contracts to build coal-to-liquid fuel plants.
analysis.headline: The bill drew eight cosponsors from both parties, but the Senate Energy Committee never took it up and it died without a vote when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have opened up Department of Energy loan guarantees and a new $200 million loan program for companies building plants that turn coal into liquid fuel, and capped those guarantees at ten projects or 100,000 barrels a day of production. It also would have let the Secretary of Defense sign contracts with private companies to build and run coal-to-liquid plants on or near military bases, extended those contracts to 25 years, authorized the Air Force to keep testing and buying coal-based jet fuel, and allowed up to 20 percent of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to be filled with coal-derived fuel.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies that would build and operate coal-to-liquid plants — chiefly coal producers and synthetic-fuel developers — gain federal backing that the private capital markets were unwilling to provide on their own: loan guarantees, planning loans, guaranteed military customers under contracts of up to 25 years, and a potential government buyer for their product in the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The Air Force also gains a certified domestic jet-fuel alternative.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Energy Policy Act of 2005 to make large-scale coal-to-liquid facilities (at least 10,000 barrels a day, using majority-domestic coal) eligible for DOE loan guarantees, with appropriations of 'such sums as are necessary' to cover the cost of the guarantees [S2][S3].
Creates a new Energy Department loan program of up to $20 million total, backed by a $200 million appropriation, to help plant developers pay for planning, permitting, and construction costs [S3].

Directs the Defense Secretary to set up regulations for building coal-to-liquid facilities on federal land, including military bases and closed installations, and lets the Defense Secretary contract with private companies to develop and operate those plants, with contract terms extended from one year to up to 25 years [S3].

Authorizes $10 million for the Air Force Research Laboratory to continue testing, qualifying, and procuring coal-based synthetic jet fuel, and allows coal-to-liquid products to make up to 20 percent of the Strategic Petroleum Reserve [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers bear the financial risk: federal loan guarantees mean the government covers the debt if the plants default, and the guarantee-cost appropriation was uncapped. The public also bears the climate cost — turning coal into liquid fuel releases roughly twice the greenhouse emissions of petroleum fuel unless the carbon is captured, and the bill did not require capture for loan eligibility. Consumers ultimately fund the reserve purchases and the military fuel contracts through the federal budget.

drawbacks.text: Federal loan guarantees for multi-billion-dollar plants put taxpayers on the hook if the projects fail commercially — the technology was largely unproven at scale in the United States, and the bill authorized 'such sums as are necessary' for the cost of the guarantees [S3].

Coal-to-liquid fuel emits roughly twice as much carbon dioxide over its life cycle as petroleum fuel unless the carbon is captured and stored; the bill mentions capture and sequestration only as optional facility components, not as a condition of the loan guarantees [S3].

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve provision would have allowed up to a fifth of the emergency oil reserve to hold a synthetic fuel with no commercial market, based only on a feasibility study rather than demonstrated need [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The energy-security argument — making transportation fuel from domestic coal instead of imported oil — is real, and the military fuel-supply provision has a genuine defense rationale. But the bill's core design shifts private investment risk onto taxpayers through open-ended loan guarantees, hands developers guaranteed government customers for up to 25 years, and does not require the carbon capture that would make the fuel comparable to petroleum on emissions. On balance it is a subsidy package for a single industry dressed as an energy-security measure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Jim Bunning introduced the bill on June 29, 2006, joined by Sens. Obama, Lugar, Burns, Pryor, Murkowski, and Bond; eight senators total signed on, six Republicans and two Democrats [S3][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day; no hearing, markup, or floor action was ever recorded [S5].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, with the bill still sitting in committee — it never received a vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers are better off because the bill died: they were never exposed to open-ended loan-guarantee risk for unproven coal-to-liquid plants, and the higher-carbon fuel never got a federal foothold. The coal and synthetic-fuel industries lost the federal financing and guaranteed customers they sought.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start — six of the eight cosponsors were Republicans and two were Democrats, including Sen. Obama — and no roll call ever occurred to test the split.

industries.note: The bill would have handed them federal loan guarantees, planning loans, and Defense Department contracts of up to 25 years — backing private markets were not providing — while taxpayers absorbed the default risk and the fuel's roughly doubled carbon emissions fell on the public.

industries.industry: U.S. Air Force and defense fuel supply
industries.note: The bill authorized $10 million to keep testing and qualifying coal-based jet fuel, supporting a domestic alternative to foreign oil for military aviation; the benefit is real but depends on the subsidized plants being built.
Open-ended appropriations for loan-guarantee costs, a $200 million loan program, and potential Strategic Petroleum Reserve purchases would all fall on the federal budget if the bill passed.
